column9: stem
column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: Looking through a microscope, you see a cell with no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles. What type of cell is it?
column28: A cell with no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles is prokaryotic. Plant and animal cells are both eukaryotic, so they always have a nucleus. A common mistake is picking plant or animal just because those are the cells you know best.
column29: Remember the class memory trick: "Pro means no."

column9: A cell that keeps its DNA inside a nucleus is called a(n) ___ cell.
column28: Eukaryotic cells keep their DNA inside a nucleus. Prokaryotic cells have no nucleus. Students often mix up the two names, so tie "pro" to "no nucleus."
column29: It is the cell type that plants, animals, and fungi are made of.

column9: A cell that has no nucleus is called a(n) ___ cell.
column28: A cell with no nucleus is prokaryotic. Bacteria and archaea are prokaryotes. A common mix-up is writing eukaryotic, which is the type WITH a nucleus.
column29: Think of the memory trick "Pro means no."

column9: Strep throat is an infection caused by Streptococcus, a kind of bacteria. What type of cells are Streptococcus?
column28: All bacteria, including Streptococcus, are prokaryotes. A common mistake is thinking that because it lives inside a human (a eukaryote), it must be eukaryotic too; where a germ lives doesn't change its cell type.
column29: What type of cell are ALL bacteria?

column9: A mushroom growing on a fallen log is a fungus. What type of cells is the mushroom made of?
column17: It is not made of cells
column28: Fungi, like plants, animals, and protists, are made of eukaryotic cells with a nucleus. Students sometimes guess prokaryotic because mushrooms grow on rotting things, but decomposers can be eukaryotes too.
column29: Fungi belong with plants, animals, and protists. Which cell type do those groups share?

column9: Which of these living things is made of eukaryotic cells?
column15: An archaean from a salt lake
column28: A deer is an animal, and animals are made of eukaryotic cells. Salmonella and cyanobacteria are bacteria, and archaea are the other group of prokaryotes. A common mistake is picking cyanobacteria because they are green like plants.
column29: Which choice is not a bacterium or an archaean?

column9: In a bacterium, the region of the cytoplasm where the DNA is concentrated is called the ___.
column28: The nucleoid is the area of a prokaryote's cytoplasm where its DNA sits. It has no membrane around it. Students often write nucleus or nucleolus, but a bacterium has neither.
column29: The word sounds like "nucleus" but means "nucleus-like."

column9: What does "membrane-bound" mean in the phrase "membrane-bound organelle"?
column14: The organelle floats with no covering
column15: The organelle is wrapped in its own membrane
column16: The organelle is attached to the cell wall
column17: The organelle is found only in bacteria
column28: A membrane-bound organelle, like the nucleus or a mitochondrion, is wrapped in its own membrane. Only eukaryotic cells have them. A common mistake is thinking it means the organelle is stuck to the cell's outer edge.
column29: "Bound" here means surrounded or enclosed.

column9: Which of these organisms is BOTH multicellular and eukaryotic?
column15: An archaean from a hot spring
column28: A dandelion is a plant made of many eukaryotic cells. An amoeba is eukaryotic but only one cell, and bacteria and archaea are single-celled prokaryotes. Students often pick the amoeba because it is eukaryotic and forget the multicellular part.
column29: Check both words: it needs a nucleus AND many cells.

column9: Which type of cell contains mitochondria, lysosomes, and a Golgi apparatus?
column28: Mitochondria, lysosomes, and the Golgi apparatus are membrane-bound organelles, which only eukaryotic cells have. A common mistake is answering both because every cell needs energy; prokaryotes do those jobs without these organelles.
column29: Are these organelles wrapped in membranes? Which cell type has that kind of organelle?

column9: Match each cell structure to its job.
column14: Flagellum :: Long, whip-like tail used for swimming
column15: Cilia :: Short, hair-like structures that move the cell or things past it
column16: Cell wall :: Stiff layer outside the cell membrane for support and protection
column17: Ribosome :: Small structure that builds proteins
column28: A flagellum is a long whip, cilia are short hairs, the cell wall is the stiff outer support layer, and ribosomes build proteins. Students often swap flagella and cilia; remember flagella are long and few, cilia are short and many.
column29: Two of these help with movement. Which one is long, and which is short?

column9: Which of these would you NEVER find inside a bacterium?
column28: Mitochondria are membrane-bound organelles, so bacteria (prokaryotes) don't have them. Bacteria do have ribosomes, DNA, and cytoplasm. A common mistake is thinking a cell can't release energy without mitochondria.
column29: Which choice is wrapped in its own membrane?

column9: A sample of pond water contains several kinds of tiny organisms. Which one is a prokaryote?
column28: Cyanobacteria are bacteria, so they are prokaryotes even though they are green and make their own food. Paramecia, amoebas, and green algae are protists with a nucleus. Students often skip cyanobacteria because they photosynthesize like plants.
column29: Look for the word that tells you which one is a kind of bacteria.

column9: What is the quickest way to tell whether a cell under a microscope is prokaryotic or eukaryotic?
column15: Check whether it has a cell membrane
column28: Having a nucleus is the key difference: eukaryotes have one, prokaryotes don't. Every cell has a cell membrane, ribosomes, and DNA, so those can't separate the two types. A common mistake is checking for DNA, but prokaryotes have DNA too.
column29: Pick the structure that only ONE of the two cell types has.

column9: Select every organism that is made of eukaryotic cells. Select all that apply.
column28: The bear (animal), bread mold (fungus), sunflower (plant), and amoeba (protist) are all eukaryotes. Bacillus is a bacterium and the archaean is the other kind of prokaryote. Students often leave out the amoeba because it is one cell, but single-celled organisms can be eukaryotic.
column29: Sort each one into a group: animal, plant, fungus, protist, bacterium, or archaean.

column9: Select every organism that is a prokaryote. Select all that apply.
column15: Lactobacillus (bacteria that turn milk into yogurt)
column28: Lactobacillus, Clostridium, and Salmonella are bacteria, so they are prokaryotes. Yeast is a fungus, a tapeworm is an animal, and Giardia is a protist, so all three are eukaryotes. A common mistake is calling yeast or Giardia prokaryotes just because they are tiny.
column29: Only bacteria and archaea are prokaryotes. Which choices are bacteria?

column9: A prokaryote is never made of many cells. The word for an organism that is made of just one cell is ___.
column20: unicellular|single-celled|single celled|one-celled|one celled|unicellular organism|single-cell|single cell|one-cell|one cell
column28: An organism made of one cell is unicellular. Prokaryotes are always unicellular; eukaryotes can be unicellular (like an amoeba) or multicellular (like you). Students sometimes write multicellular by mixing up the prefixes: uni = one, multi = many.
column29: The prefix "uni-" means one, as in unicycle.

column9: Select every structure that is a membrane-bound organelle (the kind found only in eukaryotic cells). Select all that apply.
column28: The nucleus, mitochondria, Golgi apparatus, and lysosomes are each wrapped in a membrane. Ribosomes have no membrane, which is why prokaryotes can have them. A cell wall is an outer layer, not an organelle. A common mistake is picking ribosomes because they are inside the cell.
column29: For each one, ask: is it surrounded by its own membrane?

column9: Which list contains ONLY eukaryotes?
column28: An oak (plant), a mushroom (fungus), and a human (animal) are all eukaryotes. Each other list sneaks in a bacterium or archaea, which are prokaryotes. A common mistake is choosing a list after checking only the first item.
column29: Check every item in a list. One prokaryote ruins the whole list.

column9: Which structure is found in plant cells and in most bacteria, but NOT in animal cells?
column28: Plant cells and most bacteria have a cell wall outside the cell membrane; animal cells do not. Bacteria have no nucleus, chloroplasts, or mitochondria, and animal cells do have a nucleus and mitochondria. Students often pick chloroplasts, but bacteria don't have chloroplasts.
column29: The answer must be missing from animal cells and present in a bacterium.

column9: Which choice correctly pairs each cell type with an example?
column14: Prokaryotic: a yeast cell; Eukaryotic: a bacterium
column15: Prokaryotic: a bacterium; Eukaryotic: a muscle cell
column16: Prokaryotic: a leaf cell; Eukaryotic: an archaean
column17: Prokaryotic: a muscle cell; Eukaryotic: a bacterium
column28: Bacteria are prokaryotes, and a muscle cell (from an animal) is eukaryotic. The other choices are flipped or put a eukaryote (leaf, yeast) on the prokaryote side. A common mistake is reading only the first half of the pair.
column29: Decide which example is a bacterium first.

column9: Where is most of a eukaryotic cell's DNA kept?
column28: Eukaryotic cells keep their DNA inside the nucleus. (A tiny bit is also in mitochondria and chloroplasts.) Ribosomes read the instructions to build proteins but don't store DNA. Students sometimes pick ribosomes because they work with DNA's instructions.
column29: Which structure is called the cell's control center?

column9: A student swabs a doorknob and grows small colonies of bacteria on an agar dish. Which describes each cell in those colonies?
column14: A prokaryotic cell without a nucleus
column15: A eukaryotic cell with a nucleus
column16: A plant cell with a cell wall and chloroplasts
column28: Bacteria are prokaryotes, so each cell has no nucleus. Plant and animal cells are eukaryotic and do not grow as colonies on a doorknob swab. A common mistake is thinking anything that grows in a dish must be a mold or a plant.
column29: What kind of organism did the swab pick up?

column9: Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by a bacterium. Malaria is caused by Plasmodium, a single-celled protist. Which statement is correct?
column14: The TB germ is eukaryotic, and Plasmodium is prokaryotic
column15: Both are eukaryotic because both live in humans
column16: Both are prokaryotic because both are single-celled
column17: The TB germ is prokaryotic, and Plasmodium is eukaryotic
column28: Bacteria are prokaryotes, but protists like Plasmodium have a nucleus, so they are eukaryotes. Being single-celled does not make something prokaryotic, and living in a human does not make something eukaryotic. That single-celled = prokaryote idea is the most common mistake here.
column29: Classify each one by its group (bacterium or protist), not by its size.

column9: A student stains cheek cells from inside her mouth with methylene blue and sees a dark-blue spot in the middle of each cell. What is the spot, and what does it show?
column14: A cell wall, so the cells are plant cells
column15: A ribosome, so the cells are prokaryotic
column16: The nucleus, so the cells are eukaryotic
column17: The nucleoid, so the cells are prokaryotic
column28: The dark spot is the nucleus, which shows the cheek cells are eukaryotic (they are human cells). Ribosomes are far too small to see this way, and animal cells have no cell wall. A common mistake is calling the spot a nucleoid, but nucleoids are only in prokaryotes.
column29: Cheek cells come from a human. What large structure would a human cell have in its center?

column9: In lab you look at a thin layer of onion skin under the microscope. What type of cells are you seeing?
column28: An onion is a plant, and plant cells are eukaryotic with a nucleus. Bacteria and archaea are the only prokaryotes. Students sometimes guess prokaryotic because onion skin cells look simple, but you can see a nucleus in each one when it's stained.
column29: Is an onion a plant, an animal, or a bacterium?

column9: A human skin cell is a prokaryotic cell.
column28: False. Human cells, including skin cells, have a nucleus, so they are eukaryotic. Prokaryotes are bacteria and archaea. A common mistake is thinking skin cells are simple because they sit on the outside of the body.
column29: Do human cells have a nucleus?

column9: Plant cells and bacterial cells both have a nucleus.
column28: False. Plant cells have a nucleus, but bacteria are prokaryotes and have no nucleus. They do share some things, like a cell wall, ribosomes, and a cell membrane, which is why students sometimes think they share a nucleus too.
column29: Which of the two is a prokaryote?

column9: A scientist finds a new microbe. It has a nucleus, ribosomes, and a cell membrane. How should it be classified?
column17: It can't be classified with this information
column28: The nucleus is enough to tell you it is eukaryotic. Ribosomes and a cell membrane are in every cell, so they don't help decide. A common mistake is calling any new microbe a bacterium because it is tiny.
column29: Which item on the list is found in only one of the two cell types?

column9: A human skin cell is about 30 µm across, and a bacterium sitting on it is about 3 µm long. How many times larger is the skin cell than the bacterium?
column28: 30 µm ÷ 3 µm = 10, so the skin cell is about 10 times larger. Eukaryotic cells are usually about 10 or more times larger than prokaryotes. A common mistake is subtracting (30 − 3 = 27) instead of dividing.
column29: "How many times larger" means divide the bigger size by the smaller size.

column9: Which statement correctly compares how complex the two cell types are inside?
column14: Both types are equally complex inside
column15: Prokaryotic cells are more complex, with many membrane-bound organelles
column16: Neither type has anything inside its cell membrane
column17: Eukaryotic cells are more complex, with many membrane-bound organelles
column28: Eukaryotic cells are more complex because they have a nucleus and many membrane-bound organelles. Prokaryotes are simpler and have none. A common mistake is thinking smaller means more packed with parts, but prokaryotes are small AND simple.
column29: Which cell type has organelles like mitochondria and a Golgi apparatus?

column9: A biologist looks at a bacterium with a powerful electron microscope. Which set of structures would she see?
column14: A cell membrane, cytoplasm, and a single loop of DNA
column15: A nucleus, mitochondria, and a Golgi apparatus
column16: Chloroplasts, a nucleus, and a large central vacuole
column17: Lysosomes, endoplasmic reticulum, and a nucleus
column28: A bacterium has a cell membrane, cytoplasm, and its DNA (usually one loop) loose in the cytoplasm. Every other choice includes a nucleus or membrane-bound organelles, which only eukaryotes have. A common mistake is picking the nucleus-and-mitochondria choice because those are the parts you learned first.
column29: Cross out any choice with a nucleus or a membrane-bound organelle.

column9: Giardia is a single-celled protist that can make people sick if they drink untreated stream water. Each Giardia cell has two nuclei. What type of cell is Giardia?
column28: Any cell with a nucleus (here, two) is eukaryotic. Protists are eukaryotes. A common mistake is assuming that a tiny germ that causes disease must be a bacterium.
column29: What does having a nucleus tell you?

column9: Which word describes an organism made of many cells?
column28: Multi means many, so a multicellular organism has many cells, like a tree or a person. All multicellular organisms are eukaryotes. Students sometimes mix up unicellular (one cell) and multicellular.
column29: The prefix "multi-" means many.

column9: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is a folded membrane system that helps eukaryotic cells make proteins and lipids. Would you expect to find an ER in a Salmonella bacterium?
column15: Yes, because every cell has an ER
column16: No, because the ER is a membrane-bound organelle and bacteria don't have those
column17: No, because bacteria don't make proteins
column28: Salmonella is a bacterium, and prokaryotes have no membrane-bound organelles like the ER. Bacteria still make proteins using ribosomes in their cytoplasm, so "bacteria don't make proteins" is wrong. A common mistake is thinking that because a cell does a job, it must have the same organelle we have for that job.
column29: Is the ER wrapped in membrane? Do prokaryotes have that kind of organelle?

column9: A leaf cell from a maple tree has a cell wall, a cell membrane, ribosomes, and a nucleus. Which ONE of these features shows that it is eukaryotic?
column28: Only the nucleus is found in eukaryotes and not prokaryotes. Many bacteria also have a cell wall, and all cells have ribosomes and a cell membrane. A common mistake is choosing the cell wall because it is what makes plant cells different from animal cells.
column29: Which feature would a bacterium NOT have?

column9: Which statement is true about ALL bacteria?
column28: Every bacterium is a prokaryote. Most bacteria are harmless or helpful (like the ones in yogurt), so they don't all make you sick. Bacteria have no nucleus and are single-celled. The "all bacteria are germs" idea is a common mistake.
column29: Pick the statement with no exceptions.

column9: Put these in order from smallest to largest.
column28: Ribosome (about 0.02 µm) → E. coli (about 2 µm) → cheek cell (about 60 µm) → frog egg (about 1 mm, big enough to see). A common mistake is putting the bacterium after the cheek cell; prokaryotes are usually about 10 times smaller than eukaryotic cells.
column29: A ribosome is a part INSIDE cells, so it must be the smallest. Which cells are prokaryotic?

column9: In a drop of pond water you find a green, single cell with a nucleus and several chloroplasts. What is it most likely?
column28: The nucleus and chloroplasts show it is eukaryotic, so it is an alga. Cyanobacteria are green too, but they are prokaryotes with no nucleus or chloroplasts. Viruses aren't cells at all. Students often pick cyanobacteria just because the cell is green.
column29: Which choice would have a nucleus?

column9: On the six-kingdom chart, which two kingdoms are made of prokaryotes?
column28: Archaebacteria (archaea) and Eubacteria (bacteria) are the prokaryote kingdoms. Protista, Fungi, Plantae, and Animalia are all eukaryotes. A common mistake is choosing Protista because many protists are tiny and single-celled.
column29: Look for the kingdoms with "bacteria" in their names.

column9: A tomato plant cell and a Salmonella cell would BOTH have…
column15: a nucleus and a cell membrane
column28: Every cell has a cell membrane and cytoplasm. Salmonella is a bacterium, so it has no nucleus, chloroplasts, or mitochondria. A common mistake is choosing a pair where only one of the two parts is shared.
column29: Both parts of the answer must be in the bacterium too.

column9: Sourdough bread is made with both yeast (a fungus) and Lactobacillus bacteria. Which microbe's cells have a nucleus?
column28: Yeast is a fungus, so it is eukaryotic and has a nucleus. Lactobacillus is a bacterium, a prokaryote with no nucleus. Students sometimes say neither because both are tiny and single-celled.
column29: Which one is a eukaryote?

column9: On the six-kingdom chart, which kingdom contains eukaryotes that are mostly single-celled, like amoebas and paramecia?
column28: Amoebas and paramecia are protists, a kingdom of mostly single-celled eukaryotes. Eubacteria and Archaebacteria are prokaryotes, and plants are multicellular. A common mistake is placing any single-celled organism with the bacteria.
column29: Which kingdom is eukaryotic but is not plants, animals, or fungi?

column9: A bacterium is 2 µm long. A plant cell beside it is 25 times wider. How wide is the plant cell, in µm?
column28: 2 µm × 25 = 50 µm. That fits the usual pattern: eukaryotic cells are often 10 to 100 µm, and prokaryotes are about 1 to 5 µm. A common mistake is adding (2 + 25 = 27) instead of multiplying.
column29: "25 times wider" means multiply.

column9: Which pair of organisms are BOTH eukaryotes?
column17: A sea star and a kelp (a large brown alga)
column28: A sea star is an animal and kelp is a protist (alga), so both have nucleated, eukaryotic cells. Salmonella, cyanobacteria, Staphylococcus, and Streptococcus are bacteria. A common mistake is picking kelp and a cyanobacterium because both live in water and photosynthesize.
column29: Rule out any pair that includes a bacterium.

column9: Match each feature to where it belongs in a Venn diagram comparing prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.
column16: Cell membrane :: Both prokaryotes and eukaryotes
column28: The nucleoid is where a prokaryote keeps its DNA (no nucleus). The Golgi apparatus is a membrane-bound organelle, so only eukaryotes have it. Every cell has a cell membrane. Students often put the nucleoid under eukaryotes because it sounds like nucleus.
column29: Ask for each one: is it membrane-bound, a no-nucleus feature, or something every cell needs?

column9: Match each organism to the description that fits it.
column28: E. coli is a single-celled bacterium. A paramecium is a single-celled protist with a nucleus. A maple tree has many nucleated cells. There is no multicellular prokaryote, because prokaryotes are always single-celled. The usual mistake is calling the paramecium a prokaryote because it is one cell.
column29: Decide two things for each: one cell or many? Nucleus or not?

column9: At 400×, cells in Sample 1 each show a dark, round spot. At 1000×, Sample 2 shows tiny rods with no visible structures inside. Which conclusion is best?
column15: Sample 1 is eukaryotic, and Sample 2 is most likely prokaryotic
column16: Sample 1 is prokaryotic, and Sample 2 is eukaryotic
column28: The dark spot is a nucleus, so Sample 1 is eukaryotic. Tiny rods that need 1000× and show no nucleus are most likely bacteria. A common mistake is thinking the higher magnification means the cells are bigger or more complex; it means they are smaller.
column29: What is the dark spot? And why did Sample 2 need a higher magnification?

column9: In lab you can see cheek cells clearly at 100× to 400×, but bacteria from yogurt look like tiny specks until you use 1000×. Why?
column14: Bacteria are clear and have no DNA to stain
column15: Cheek cells are prokaryotic, so they are larger
column16: Bacteria (about 1–5 µm) are much smaller than cheek cells (about 60 µm)
column17: Yogurt bacteria are dead, so they shrink
column28: Prokaryotes are usually about 10 or more times smaller than eukaryotic cells, so you need more magnification to see them. Bacteria do have DNA, and cheek cells are eukaryotic, not prokaryotic. A common mistake is mixing up which cell type is the larger one.
column29: What does needing more magnification tell you about an object's size?

column9: A plant cell is 60 µm long. A bacterium is 1.5 µm long. How many bacteria lined up end to end would stretch across the plant cell?
column28: 60 µm ÷ 1.5 µm = 40 bacteria. This shows how much bigger eukaryotic cells usually are. A common mistake is multiplying (60 × 1.5 = 90) instead of dividing.
column29: Divide the plant cell's length by the length of one bacterium.

column9: Which statement describes a DIFFERENCE between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, not a similarity?
column14: Both types of cells have ribosomes
column15: Both types of cells have cytoplasm
column16: Both types of cells use DNA as their genetic material
column17: Only eukaryotic cells have membrane-bound organelles
column28: Membrane-bound organelles are found only in eukaryotes, so that is a difference. Ribosomes, DNA, and cytoplasm are found in both, so those are similarities. A common mistake is choosing any true statement without checking whether it compares or contrasts.
column29: Three of the choices start with "Both." What does that tell you?

column9: Which statement correctly compares the DNA of prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells?
column14: Both keep their DNA in a nucleus, but prokaryotes have more chromosomes
column15: Eukaryotes keep most of their DNA in a nucleus as several straight chromosomes; prokaryotes usually have one loop-shaped chromosome in the cytoplasm
column16: Prokaryotes keep their DNA in a nucleus, and eukaryotes keep it in the cytoplasm
column17: Only eukaryotes have DNA; prokaryotes use proteins instead
column28: Both cell types use DNA. Eukaryotic DNA is in a nucleus as linear (straight) chromosomes; prokaryotic DNA is usually one circular chromosome loose in the cytoplasm (the nucleoid). A common mistake is flipping where each cell keeps its DNA.
column29: Which cell type has no nucleus to hold its DNA?

column9: A scientist finds a single-celled microbe in the very salty water of the Great Salt Lake. It has no nucleus, but tests show it is not a bacterium. What is it most likely?
column28: A cell with no nucleus is a prokaryote, and the only prokaryotes that are not bacteria are archaea, which often live in extreme places like salty lakes and hot springs. Protists, fungi, and plants all have a nucleus. A common mistake is picking protist because it is single-celled.
column29: There are two groups of prokaryotes. If it is not one, it must be the other.

column9: Put the steps for classifying an unknown cell from a pond sample in order.
column14: Decide whether the cell is prokaryotic or eukaryotic
column15: Place a drop of the sample on a slide, add a stain, and add a coverslip
column16: Look for a nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles
column17: Focus on low power, then switch to high power or oil immersion
column28: Make the slide → focus from low to high power → look for a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles → decide the cell type. A common mistake is deciding before looking; your conclusion has to come from the evidence.
column29: You can't look for a nucleus until the slide is made and in focus.

column9: Which description best fits a typical prokaryotic cell?
column14: Small, a nucleus, and no ribosomes
column15: Large (about 50 µm), a nucleus, mitochondria, and a Golgi apparatus
column16: Large, no DNA, and many membrane-bound organelles
column17: Small (about 1–5 µm), no nucleus, DNA in the cytoplasm, ribosomes, often a cell wall
column28: Prokaryotes are small, have no nucleus, keep DNA in the cytoplasm, have ribosomes, and often have a cell wall. The large cell with a nucleus and mitochondria is a eukaryotic cell. Every cell has DNA and ribosomes, so the "no ribosomes" and "no DNA" choices can't describe any real cell. A common mistake is picking the other "small" choice without noticing it has a nucleus.
column29: Check each part of the description, not just the size.

column9: Select every structure that a human liver cell has but a bacterium does NOT. Select all that apply.
column28: The nucleus, mitochondria, ER, and Golgi apparatus are membrane-bound, so only eukaryotes like liver cells have them. Ribosomes and a cell membrane are in both cell types. A common mistake is picking ribosomes, but ribosomes have no membrane and are found in bacteria.
column29: Pick only the membrane-bound parts.

column9: Select every statement that is true of ALL prokaryotes. Select all that apply.
column28: All prokaryotes are single-celled, lack a nucleus, have ribosomes, and have DNA. No prokaryote has chloroplasts (even cyanobacteria photosynthesize without them), and only some have a flagellum. A common mistake is choosing flagellum because many textbook bacteria are drawn with one.
column29: "ALL" means no exceptions. Some prokaryotes swim and some don't.

column9: Your large intestine is home to trillions of bacteria. Does that make you prokaryotic, eukaryotic, or both?
column14: You are both, because bacteria are part of your body
column15: Your own cells are eukaryotic; the gut bacteria are separate prokaryotic organisms living in you
column16: Your gut cells are prokaryotic, and the rest of your cells are eukaryotic
column17: You are prokaryotic, because there are so many bacteria in you
column28: Every one of your own cells (gut cells included) is eukaryotic. The bacteria are different organisms that live inside you, and they stay prokaryotic. A common mistake is thinking living together changes the cell type.
column29: Are the bacteria made from your cells, or are they their own organisms?

column9: Which pair of cells would BOTH have a cell wall AND a nucleus?
column14: A bacterium and an oak leaf cell
column15: A human skin cell and a mushroom cell
column17: An oak leaf cell and a mushroom cell
column28: Plant cells and fungal cells both have a cell wall and a nucleus. Bacteria and archaea have no nucleus, and human cells have no cell wall. A common mistake is choosing the bacterium pair because bacteria have cell walls, forgetting the nucleus part.
column29: Check both features for both cells in each pair.

column9: A cell has a nucleus and mitochondria, but no cell wall and no chloroplasts. Which organism could it come from?
column28: A nucleus means eukaryotic, and no cell wall rules out plants and fungi, so it is an animal cell, like a dog's. A bacterium has no nucleus or mitochondria. A common mistake is picking the mushroom, but fungal cells have cell walls.
column29: First decide prokaryote or eukaryote, then use the cell wall clue.

column9: Euglena is a single cell that swims with a flagellum and makes food with chloroplasts. It also has a nucleus. A classmate says it is a bacterium because it is single-celled and has a flagellum. What is the best response?
column14: It is a plant cell, because only plants have chloroplasts
column15: It is eukaryotic, because it has a nucleus (and chloroplasts); being single-celled with a flagellum doesn't make it a bacterium
column16: The classmate is right, because only bacteria have flagella
column17: The classmate is right, because all single-celled organisms are prokaryotes
column28: The nucleus and chloroplasts are membrane-bound, so Euglena is a eukaryote (a protist). Eukaryotes can be single-celled and can have flagella. It isn't a plant, because protists can have chloroplasts too. The common mistake is classifying by size or by how it moves.
column29: Which feature is the deciding one between prokaryote and eukaryote?

column9: A student sorted cards into a "prokaryotes" pile: Salmonella, Lactobacillus, amoeba, and cyanobacteria. Which card is in the wrong pile?
column28: An amoeba is a protist with a nucleus, so it is eukaryotic. Salmonella, Lactobacillus, and cyanobacteria are all bacteria. A common mistake is pulling out cyanobacteria because they photosynthesize, but they are still bacteria.
column29: Three of the cards are bacteria. Which one isn't?

column9: Which statement about ribosomes in the two cell types is correct?
column15: Both have ribosomes attached to a rough ER
column16: Both have ribosomes, but only eukaryotic cells can have ribosomes attached to a rough ER
column28: Every cell needs ribosomes to make proteins, so both types have them. Only eukaryotes have an ER for some ribosomes to attach to; in prokaryotes they are all free in the cytoplasm. A common mistake is thinking ribosomes are membrane-bound organelles, so prokaryotes can't have them.
column29: Does a prokaryote have an endoplasmic reticulum?

column9: The head of a pin is about 1,500 µm wide. How many 3-µm bacteria lined up end to end would fit across it?
column28: 1,500 µm ÷ 3 µm = 500 bacteria. Prokaryotes are so small that hundreds fit across a pinhead. A common mistake is multiplying the two numbers instead of dividing.
column29: Divide the width of the pinhead by the size of one bacterium.

column9: Human sperm cells and many bacteria both swim using a flagellum. What does this tell you about using a flagellum to classify a cell?
column14: Any cell with a flagellum must be eukaryotic
column16: Any cell with a flagellum must be prokaryotic
column17: A flagellum can't tell you the cell type, because some prokaryotes and some eukaryotes have one
column28: Because both cell types can have flagella, a flagellum alone can't separate them; you need to look for a nucleus. Sperm cells are human cells, so they are eukaryotic. A common mistake is thinking flagella belong only to bacteria.
column29: If both cell types can have it, can it tell them apart?

column9: Based on size alone, select every cell that is most likely prokaryotic. Select all that apply.
column28: Prokaryotes are usually about 1–5 µm (some are smaller), while most eukaryotic cells are about 10–100 µm. So A and B are most likely prokaryotes. Size is good evidence but not proof; the nucleus is what decides. A common mistake is choosing C because 20 sounds small.
column29: Typical prokaryotes are only a few micrometers long.

column9: The idea that mitochondria and chloroplasts were once free-living prokaryotes that ended up living inside larger cells is called the ___ theory.
column28: The endosymbiotic theory says mitochondria and chloroplasts came from prokaryotes that lived inside bigger cells. "Endo" means inside and "symbiosis" means living together. Students sometimes write "cell theory," but that is a different idea from LT1.
column29: Endo = inside; symbiosis = living together.

column9: A student's Venn diagram puts "nucleus" in the middle section, as something BOTH prokaryotes and eukaryotes have. What correction should be made?
column15: Move it to the eukaryotes-only side
column16: Move it to the prokaryotes-only side
column17: Remove it, because neither cell type has a nucleus
column28: Only eukaryotic cells have a nucleus; that is the main difference between the two types. Prokaryotes have a nucleoid region instead. A common mistake is treating the nucleoid as a nucleus.
column29: Does a bacterium have a nucleus?

column9: Blue cheese gets its veins from Penicillium mold, and the cheese is made with Lactococcus bacteria. Which of these microbes can have mitochondria?
column28: Penicillium is a fungus, a eukaryote, so it has mitochondria. Lactococcus is a bacterium, a prokaryote, so it has no membrane-bound organelles. A common mistake is thinking every living cell needs mitochondria to get energy.
column29: Mitochondria are membrane-bound. Which microbe is a eukaryote?

column9: Select every pair in which BOTH organisms are prokaryotes. Select all that apply.
column19: Helicobacter (stomach bacteria) and a methane-making archaean
column28: Staphylococcus, Bacillus, Helicobacter, Rhizobium, and Vibrio are bacteria, and archaea are prokaryotes too. Yeast and mushrooms are fungi, and amoebas and paramecia are protists, so those pairs contain eukaryotes. A common mistake is choosing the amoeba and paramecium pair because both are single cells.
column29: Both organisms in the pair must be bacteria or archaea.

column9: Which structure would be USELESS for telling a bacterium apart from a yeast cell, because both cells have it?
column28: Yeast is a fungus, and fungal cells have cell walls, just like most bacteria. The nucleus, mitochondria, and ER are only in the yeast, so those WOULD tell them apart. A common mistake is thinking only plants and bacteria have cell walls.
column29: Fungal cells have something in common with plant cells and bacteria on the outside.

column9: In a eukaryotic cell, the DNA stays inside the nucleus while ribosomes build proteins out in the cytoplasm. In a bacterium, where are the DNA and the ribosomes?
column14: The DNA is in the nucleus and the ribosomes are in the cytoplasm
column15: Together in the same space, the cytoplasm
column28: A bacterium has no nucleus, so its DNA and ribosomes share the cytoplasm. A eukaryotic cell keeps them in separate compartments. A common mistake is giving a bacterium a nucleus or mitochondria.
column29: Does a bacterium have any compartment to keep its DNA apart?

column9: A classmate says, "Viruses are prokaryotes because they are tiny and have no nucleus." What is the best response?
column14: The classmate is right, because anything without a nucleus is a prokaryote
column15: Viruses aren't cells at all, so they are neither prokaryotes nor eukaryotes
column16: Viruses are prokaryotes only when they infect bacteria
column17: Viruses are eukaryotes, because they infect eukaryotic cells
column28: Prokaryote and eukaryote are types of cells. Viruses have no cell membrane, cytoplasm, or ribosomes of their own, so they aren't cells and don't fit either group. A common mistake is lumping viruses in with bacteria because both are germs.
column29: Prokaryote and eukaryote are names for kinds of what?

column9: The double membrane that surrounds the nucleus of a eukaryotic cell is called the nuclear ___.
column28: The nuclear envelope (also called the nuclear membrane) wraps the nucleus. Prokaryotes don't have one, so their DNA sits in the cytoplasm. Students sometimes write "wall," but walls are outside the cell membrane, not around the nucleus.
column29: It's like an envelope holding a letter (the DNA).

column9: Tube A holds Bacillus bacteria and Tube B holds paramecia. You add a dye that stains only nuclei and look at a drop from each tube. What should you see?
column14: Stained nuclei in the Bacillus only
column16: Stained nuclei in the paramecia only
column28: Paramecia are protists (eukaryotes) with a nucleus, so they stain. Bacillus is a bacterium with no nucleus, so nothing stains. A common mistake is expecting the DNA in the nucleoid to show as a nucleus; there is no nuclear envelope around it.
column29: Which tube has cells with a nucleus to stain?

column9: Data from four cells — Cell A: 3 µm, cell wall, no nucleus. Cell B: 30 µm, cell wall, nucleus, chloroplasts. Cell C: 15 µm, no cell wall, nucleus, mitochondria. Cell D: 8 µm, cell wall, nucleus, no chloroplasts. Select every cell that is eukaryotic. Select all that apply.
column28: B, C, and D each have a nucleus, so they are eukaryotic (B looks like a plant cell, C an animal cell, D a fungus like yeast). A has no nucleus, so it is prokaryotic. A common mistake is leaving out D because it is small and has a cell wall; the nucleus decides.
column29: Ignore the cell wall and size for a moment. Which column decides the type?

column9: A student says, "Cyanobacteria do photosynthesis, so they must have chloroplasts and be eukaryotic." Which response is best?
column14: The student is right, because anything green is a plant
column15: The student is right, because only eukaryotes can photosynthesize
column16: Cyanobacteria are eukaryotic only during the day, when they photosynthesize
column17: Cyanobacteria photosynthesize using membranes in their cytoplasm; they have no nucleus or chloroplasts, so they are prokaryotes
column28: Cyanobacteria are bacteria. They carry out photosynthesis without chloroplasts, using folded membranes in their cytoplasm, and they have no nucleus. Doing a job (photosynthesis) doesn't prove a cell has the organelle we use for it. That is the student's mistake.
column29: Do cyanobacteria have a nucleus? What does that make them?

column9: The antibiotic penicillin kills many bacteria by stopping them from building their cell walls. Why doesn't penicillin damage your own cells in the same way?
column15: Human cells have no cell membrane
column16: Human cells are prokaryotic, so the drug can't enter
column17: Human cells are animal cells and have no cell wall
column28: Penicillin targets something bacteria have and animal cells don't: a cell wall. Human cells have a cell membrane but no wall, so there's nothing for the drug to block. A common mistake is saying human cells are prokaryotic; they are eukaryotic.
column29: What structure does the drug attack? Do human cells have it?

column9: Put the steps of the endosymbiotic theory for the origin of mitochondria in order.
column14: Over many generations, the small cell became a mitochondrion that can no longer live on its own
column15: A large cell engulfed a small prokaryote that could use oxygen to release energy
column16: The host cell protected the small cell, and the small cell supplied extra energy
column17: The small prokaryote was not digested and kept living inside the larger cell
column28: Engulfed → not digested, kept living inside → both cells benefited → over many generations it became a mitochondrion. A common mistake is putting the teamwork step before the small cell survived; it had to stay alive inside first.
column29: Start with the moment the big cell swallowed the small one.

column9: Some antibiotics that block bacterial ribosomes can also cause side effects by slowing down the ribosomes inside human mitochondria. Which idea best explains this?
column14: Mitochondrial ribosomes resemble bacterial ribosomes, which supports the idea that mitochondria came from bacteria
column15: Mitochondria are made in the nucleus, so they copy human ribosomes
column16: Human mitochondria are prokaryotic cells living in the cytoplasm today
column17: The antibiotic turns human cells into prokaryotes
column28: Mitochondria have their own small ribosomes that are built like bacterial ones, so a drug aimed at bacterial ribosomes can affect them too. This fits the endosymbiotic theory that mitochondria descended from bacteria. Saying mitochondria are prokaryotic cells today goes too far: they are organelles now, not separate living organisms.
column29: What would you expect mitochondria to keep if they came from bacteria long ago?

column9: At 1000×, a microscope's field of view is 180 µm across. A student counts about 90 bacteria lined up end to end across the field. About how long is one bacterium, in µm?
column28: 180 µm ÷ 90 bacteria = 2 µm each, a typical size for a prokaryote like E. coli. A common mistake is dividing the wrong way (90 ÷ 180 = 0.5) or using the 1000× magnification in the math; the field width is already the real size.
column29: Divide the field's width by the number of cells that span it.

column9: Imagine a eukaryotic cell and a prokaryotic cell that are both cube-shaped. The eukaryotic cell is 10 times wider. How many times greater is its volume?
column28: Volume of a cube = side × side × side, so 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000 times the volume. That huge inside space is one reason eukaryotes need organelles and internal membranes to organize the work. A common mistake is answering 10 (width only) or 100 (area only).
column29: A cube has three dimensions. Each one is 10 times bigger.

column9: Select every observation that, by itself, tells you a cell is eukaryotic. Select all that apply.
column28: A nucleus, mitochondria, and a Golgi apparatus are only found in eukaryotes, so any one of them is proof. Ribosomes are in all cells, and cell walls and flagella show up in some prokaryotes and some eukaryotes. A common mistake is picking cell wall, which bacteria have too.
column29: For each feature, ask: could a bacterium ever have this?

column9: A student argues, "All multicellular organisms are eukaryotes, so all eukaryotes must be multicellular." Which evidence best shows the second part is wrong?
column15: Bacteria are single-celled and have no nucleus
column16: Oak trees are multicellular and have a nucleus in each cell
column17: Amoebas and paramecia are single-celled organisms that have a nucleus
column28: Amoebas and paramecia are eukaryotes made of one cell, which disproves "all eukaryotes are multicellular." Bacteria and archaea are prokaryotes, so they say nothing about eukaryotes. The oak tree fits the claim, so it can't disprove it. A common mistake is flipping a true statement around and assuming it stays true.
column29: You need an example of a eukaryote that is NOT multicellular.

column9: In a eukaryotic cell, lysosomes keep strong digestive enzymes inside their own membrane. Why is having separate compartments like this an advantage that prokaryotes don't have?
column14: It lets the cell skip having a cell membrane
column15: It keeps harmful enzymes away from the rest of the cell and lets different jobs happen in separate spaces at once
column16: It makes the cell smaller than a bacterium
column17: It means the cell no longer needs DNA
column28: Membrane-bound compartments let a eukaryotic cell keep reactions apart, so digestive enzymes don't damage other parts and many jobs can run side by side. Prokaryotes have one shared space, the cytoplasm. A common mistake is thinking compartments make cells smaller; eukaryotes are usually much bigger.
column29: What would happen if digestive enzymes floated loose in the whole cell?

column9: How many of these organisms are prokaryotes? E. coli, brewer's yeast, Salmonella, an amoeba, a cyanobacterium, a mushroom, a hot-spring archaean
column28: Prokaryotes: E. coli, Salmonella, the cyanobacterium (all bacteria), and the archaean = 4. Yeast and the mushroom are fungi, and the amoeba is a protist, so they are eukaryotes. A common mistake is skipping the archaean or the cyanobacterium.
column29: Count only the bacteria and archaea.

column9: How many of these structures are found ONLY in eukaryotic cells? lysosome, ribosome, smooth endoplasmic reticulum, cell membrane, nucleus, cytoplasm
column28: Lysosome, smooth ER, and nucleus are membrane-bound, so only eukaryotes have them = 3. Ribosomes, the cell membrane, and cytoplasm are in every cell. A common mistake is counting ribosomes, which are not wrapped in a membrane.
column29: Count only the structures wrapped in their own membrane.

column9: An unknown cell is 1.5 µm long and has ribosomes, a cell membrane, and a cell wall. A student says, "It must be prokaryotic because it's so tiny." What is the best evaluation of this claim?
column14: Its size is good evidence, but the claim would be stronger after checking for a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles
column15: The claim is wrong, because a cell wall means it is a plant cell
column16: The claim is proven, because any cell under 10 µm is prokaryotic
column17: The claim is wrong, because ribosomes are found only in eukaryotes
column28: Most prokaryotes are 1–5 µm, so the size fits, but size alone isn't proof; a few eukaryotic cells are tiny too. The deciding test is whether it has a nucleus. A cell wall doesn't mean plant, and ribosomes are in all cells. A common mistake is treating one clue as proof.
column29: Is size the feature that defines a prokaryote, or is something else?

column9: According to the endosymbiotic theory, chloroplasts came from which kind of prokaryote that was taken in by an early eukaryotic cell?
column14: A photosynthetic bacterium, like today's cyanobacteria
column16: An archaean from a hot spring
column28: Chloroplasts do photosynthesis, so the theory says they came from photosynthetic bacteria similar to modern cyanobacteria. Archaea and disease-causing bacteria don't photosynthesize, and yeast is a eukaryote, not a prokaryote. A common mistake is picking yeast without noticing the question asks for a prokaryote.
column29: What job do chloroplasts do? Which prokaryotes already do that job?

column9: A data table — Organism 1: nucleus YES, many cells. Organism 2: nucleus NO, one cell. Organism 3: nucleus YES, one cell. Organism 4: nucleus NO, one cell. Which conclusion is supported by this data?
column14: Organisms without a nucleus are multicellular
column15: Every organism with a nucleus is multicellular
column16: The organisms without a nucleus are all single-celled, but having a nucleus doesn't tell you how many cells an organism has
column17: The number of cells decides whether an organism is prokaryotic or eukaryotic
column28: Organisms 2 and 4 (no nucleus) are single-celled, while organisms with a nucleus include one with many cells (1) and one with a single cell (3). So the nucleus, not the cell count, decides the type. A common mistake is ignoring Organism 3 and concluding all eukaryotes are multicellular.
column29: Look closely at Organism 3. What does it show?

column9: Pond survey — V: nucleus, flagellum, 15 µm. W: nucleus, cilia, 120 µm. X: no nucleus, flagellum, 2 µm. Y: no nucleus, green, does photosynthesis, 4 µm. Z: nucleus, chloroplasts, 30 µm. Select every organism that is a prokaryote. Select all that apply.
column28: X and Y have no nucleus, so they are prokaryotes (Y is probably a cyanobacterium). V, W, and Z all have a nucleus, so they are eukaryotes, even V, which has a flagellum like X. A common mistake is choosing V because of the flagellum, or leaving out Y because it photosynthesizes.
column29: Use only the nucleus column to decide.

column9: A tuberculosis bacterium invades a human lung cell. Which choice names a structure BOTH cells have, and a structure ONLY the lung cell has?
column14: Both: mitochondria; Only the lung cell: a cell wall
column15: Both: ribosomes; Only the lung cell: a nucleus
column16: Both: a nucleus; Only the lung cell: ribosomes
column17: Both: a cell wall; Only the lung cell: cytoplasm
column28: Every cell has ribosomes, but only the eukaryotic lung cell has a nucleus. Bacteria have no nucleus or mitochondria, and human cells have no cell wall. A common mistake is reading only the first half of each choice.
column29: Check both halves: the shared part must be in the bacterium too.

column9: A cell is found to have a cell wall, ribosomes, DNA, and a cell membrane. Nothing else is known about it yet. Select every kind of cell it COULD be. Select all that apply.
column28: Bacteria, most archaea, plant cells, and fungal cells all have cell walls plus ribosomes, DNA, and a membrane. Animal cells have no cell wall, and a virus isn't a cell at all. A common mistake is choosing only the bacterium or only the plant cell; without knowing about a nucleus, you can't narrow it down further.
column29: Which cells have a cell wall? Which choice isn't a cell at all?

column9: Mitochondria are wrapped in two membranes. How does the endosymbiotic theory explain the two membranes?
column14: The inner membrane came from the engulfed prokaryote's own membrane, and the outer one came from the host cell wrapping around it
column15: Both membranes were made later by the Golgi apparatus
column16: Mitochondria grew a second membrane to protect the nucleus
column17: The two membranes came from two different host cells
column28: When the large cell engulfed the prokaryote, the prokaryote kept its own cell membrane (inner) and was wrapped in a piece of the host's membrane (outer). That double layer is evidence for the theory. A common mistake is thinking the extra membrane was added later for protection.
column29: Picture the big cell wrapping its membrane around a small cell that already had a membrane.

column9: Doctors have many drugs that kill bacteria without hurting patients, but far fewer drugs for fungal infections like athlete's foot. Which explanation is best?
column14: Human cells have cell walls that protect them from antibacterial drugs
column15: Fungal cells have no cell membrane
column16: Fungi are eukaryotes like us, so their cells share more structures with human cells, and drugs that harm them are more likely to harm us
column17: Fungi are prokaryotes, so they have no structures for drugs to target
column28: Bacteria are prokaryotes with many differences from our cells (no nucleus, different ribosomes, cell walls), so it's easy to target them safely. Fungi have a nucleus, mitochondria, and other features like ours, so it's harder to find a drug that hits only the fungus. A common mistake is thinking fungi are prokaryotes.
column29: The more alike two cells are, the harder it is to hurt one without the other.

column9: Under a 1000× microscope, the image of a bacterium is 3 mm long. How long is the real bacterium, in µm? (1 mm = 1,000 µm)
column28: Convert first: 3 mm = 3,000 µm. Then divide by the magnification: 3,000 µm ÷ 1000 = 3 µm, a typical prokaryote size. A common mistake is forgetting to convert millimeters and answering 0.003.
column29: Change the image size to µm, then undo the magnification by dividing.

column9: A student's Venn diagram reads — Prokaryotes only: no nucleus, cell wall, unicellular. Eukaryotes only: nucleus, membrane-bound organelles, multicellular. Both: DNA, ribosomes, cell membrane. Which TWO entries in the "Prokaryotes only" section are placed wrong?
column28: Cell walls are found in some prokaryotes AND some eukaryotes (plants, fungi), and some eukaryotes (amoebas, yeast) are unicellular, so both belong in the middle. "No nucleus" truly is prokaryotes-only. A common mistake is assuming anything bacteria have must be prokaryotes-only.
column29: For each entry, ask whether ANY eukaryote also has it.

column9: Scientists find a single-celled organism that has a nucleus but no mitochondria. A classmate says it must be a prokaryote because it is missing mitochondria. Which response is best?
column14: It is a eukaryote, because having a nucleus is the defining feature; missing mitochondria doesn't make it a prokaryote
column15: It is neither, because it breaks the rules
column16: It is a prokaryote, because it is single-celled
column17: The classmate is right, because all eukaryotes have mitochondria
column28: The nucleus is what makes a cell eukaryotic. A few eukaryotes (like Giardia) have lost their mitochondria but still have a nucleus. Being single-celled doesn't make it a prokaryote either. A common mistake is treating every eukaryote feature as required.
column29: Which feature is the definition of a eukaryote?

column9: Match each observation to the conclusion it best supports.
column14: The cell has a nuclear envelope :: The cell is eukaryotic, but you can't tell which kingdom yet
column15: The cell is 1 µm long with its DNA loose in the cytoplasm :: The cell is prokaryotic
column16: The cell has a cell wall, a nucleus, and chloroplasts :: The cell is a plant or algae cell
column17: The cell has a nucleus but no cell wall or chloroplasts :: The cell is most likely an animal cell
column18: The cell has ribosomes :: You can't tell; all cells have them
column28: A nuclear envelope means eukaryotic. Tiny size with loose DNA means prokaryotic. Wall + nucleus + chloroplasts points to a plant or alga, and nucleus with no wall points to an animal cell. Ribosomes are in every cell, so they prove nothing. A common mistake is treating ribosomes as evidence of a eukaryote.
column29: Start with the observation that can't decide anything.

column9: Select every TRUE statement comparing prokaryotes and eukaryotes. Select all that apply.
column28: Both cell types have ribosomes, only eukaryotes form multicellular organisms, and prokaryotes are usually much smaller. Plants and fungi have cell walls too, both types have DNA, and both types can have flagella. A common mistake is picking "only prokaryotes have cell walls" because bacteria are famous for cell walls.
column29: Watch for the word "only." One counterexample makes the statement false.
